claims.text: In-situ laser re-melting after each deposited layer reduces fabrication-induced defects in additively manufactured high-entropy alloys.
In-situ laser re-melting after each deposited layer reduces residual stresses in additively manufactured high-entropy alloys.
Reducing defects and residual stresses through layer re-melting improves dimensional precision and mechanical integrity.
As-built additively manufactured high-entropy-alloy components commonly contain porosity, unmelted regions, non-uniform microstructures, and residual stresses.
The defects and residual stresses in the as-built components lead to dimensional inaccuracies.
The proposed intervention is a lower-power, adjusted-scan-speed laser re-melting pass immediately after each layer is deposited.
An appropriately adjusted re-melting pass can re-melt the layer surface without excessive heat input.
Layer re-melting promotes grain refinement.
Layer re-melting reduces local thermal gradients.
Layer re-melting consolidates the melt pool by eliminating porosity and unmelted regions.
Melt-pool consolidation and defect elimination mitigate residual-stress build-up.
Residual-stress build-up is a primary mediator of dimensional inaccuracy.
Re-melting temporarily raises the local temperature enough to partially homogenize the microstructure and heal minor defects.
Reduced residual stress diminishes shrinkage and warping that compromise dimensional precision.
The microstructure produced by layer re-melting benefits mechanical integrity.
Compared with standard additive manufacturing without re-melting, re-melted components will have smaller deviations from their design dimensions.
Compared with the baseline, re-melted components will have higher tensile strength and better ductility.
Compared with the baseline, re-melted components will have a lower density of fabrication-induced defects.
The intervention is most applicable when severe thermal gradients produce notable porosity and residual stresses.
High-melting-point alloys or alloys requiring substantially different thermal profiles may require different re-melting parameters.
